newsitem.title: UK: UK firm eyes cure for faded flowers and jetlag.
newsitem.headline: UK firm eyes cure for faded flowers and jetlag.

text.p: A British firm developing a machine to rid homes of radon gas says it may have stumbled on a way of reviving wilted flowers and even of curing jet lag.

Engineers at Radiation Control Systems, based in Frome, western England, left a prototype electron generator running overnight in a warm office near a vase of fading flowers. By the next morning the flowers had revived and were bolt upright.
Repeated experiments produced similar results and the firm is now negotiating to sell the machine to the flower industry, where wastage at the retail stage can reach 30 percent.
Keith Foster, the owner of the firm, says it appears that the stream of electrons emitted by the low-voltage machine increases the metabolic rate of plants.
"A good analogy would be a car battery which has become discharged and is recharged. We charge them back up again," he told Reuters.

Even more intriguingly, Foster says the machine also appears to work on human beings. A colleague who had returned from a tiring overseas business trip perked up after sitting in the electron stream for an hour and was able to go on working.
"At this point it's not good science...but it's a general indication that the machine works," said Foster, whose firm is looking for a bigger partner to market the device.

Phil Gates of the Biological Sciences Department of Durham University, who is planning a series of experiments to try to verify Foster's findings, said he could not offer any scientific explanation for the reported effects.
"But a lot of interesting scientific discoveries start off accidentally," Gates said. "Serendipity can have a lot to do with it."
Foster's firm developed the machine, dubbed the Progenitor, to clear buildings of alpha radiation caused by naturally occurring radon gas, which scientists suspect causes cancer.
